title: Implement heap sort using a binary heap, explain the heapify and sort-down phases, and analyse its complexity and stability.
keyPoints: Heap sort builds a max-heap, then repeatedly swaps the root maximum to the end and sifts down over the shrinking heap.
A binary heap is represented in the array: children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, parent at (i-1)/2.
Building the heap by sifting down from the last parent toward the root is O(n), not O(n log n).
The sort-down phase extracts n elements at O(log n) each, giving O(n log n) total in all cases.
Heap sort is in-place with O(1) extra space, and it has no quadratic worst case like quick sort.
It is not stable because swapping distant elements reorders equal keys.
Its cache-unfriendly access pattern makes it slower in practice than quick sort, so its niche is guaranteed O(n log n) with constant space.

s1_definition.oneliner: Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root maximum to the end and sift down over the shrinking heap.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Heap sort** – a comparison-based, in-place sort using a binary max-heap stored directly in the array.
- **Build heap** – sift down every non-leaf node from the last parent toward the root; this is O(n).
- **Sort down** – swap the root (maximum) to the end, shrink the heap, sift down the new root; O(n log n) total.
- **In-place** – uses O(1) extra space; no auxiliary buffer needed.
- **Not stable** – swapping distant elements can reorder equal keys.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranges transaction amounts into a tournament bracket where every manager holds an amount at least as big as the two people below them, so the biggest amount sits at the top. The clerk takes the top amount (the largest), places it at the end of the sorted list, then lets the replacement sink to its proper level. She repeats until every amount has been extracted in descending order.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Binary Max-Heap in Array:

  Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5
  Value: [80] [50] [70] [20] [40] [10]

            80
          /    \
        50      70
       / \     /
      20  40  10

  Sort-Down Phase:
  Step 1: Swap 80 with last (10), sift down 10
    [10, 50, 70, 20, 40 | 80]  -> sift 10 -> [70, 50, 10, 20, 40 | 80]
  Step 2: Swap 70 with last active (40), sift down 40
    [40, 50, 10, 20 | 70, 80]  -> sift 40 -> [50, 40, 10, 20 | 70, 80]
  ... continue until sorted:
    [10, 20, 40, 50, 70, 80]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Heap sort is a comparison-based, in-place sort built on a binary max-heap stored directly in the array. It has two phases: build the max-heap in O(n) time, then repeatedly extract the maximum by swapping it to the end and sifting the new root down, which takes O(n log n) total. This O(n log n) holds in the best, average, and worst case with O(1) extra space.

The sift-down procedure is the core logic: it takes a node that may violate the heap property, compares it against its larger child, and swaps it down until the property is restored. Building the heap by sifting down from the last parent is O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom with short sift distances.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, heap sort is reserved for memory-constrained nodes that cannot afford merge sort's O(n) buffer and cannot risk quick sort's quadratic worst case. Its cache-unfriendly access pattern makes it slower than quick sort in practice, which is why it is not the default.

The heap structure itself is more commonly used as a priority queue. Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap powering Dijkstra's algorithm, merge-K-sorted-lists, and task scheduling, which is where heaps really earn their keep in production.

Remember one sentence: heap sort builds a max-heap in-place, extracts the maximum repeatedly, and guarantees O(n log n) with O(1) space, but cache-unfriendly access keeps it niche compared to quick sort.
